title: How do social media feed algorithms affect attitudes and behavior in an election campaign?
type: Peer-reviewed randomized field experiment; original abstract verified through Europe PMC
findings: Assigning consenting Facebook and Instagram users to reverse-chronological feeds during the 2020 election reduced platform time and activity and altered exposure. Political and untrustworthy content increased on both platforms; other exposure measures changed in different directions. No significant effects on issue polarization, affective polarization, political knowledge, or other key attitudes were found over the study period.
limitations: An intervention on consenting users over three months, not an estimate of all accumulated platform effects. Chronological ordering retains user-selected sources. Original abstract was read; no reanalysis of underlying data was conducted.

stats.denominator: Duration of the experimental feed intervention; not a population share

title: Like-minded sources on Facebook are prevalent but not polarizing
type: Peer-reviewed randomized field experiment and exposure analysis; abstract and main-text methods/findings read
findings: Reducing exposure to like-minded sources by approximately one-third among 23,377 participants altered exposure and reduced uncivil content, but produced no measurable effects on eight preregistered attitude outcomes. Replacements were not exclusively cross-cutting sources. The paper discloses its Meta collaboration and academic publication-control arrangements.
limitations: The tested demotion did not remove the entire like-minded information diet. Participants could receive information elsewhere. Results concern the 2020 Facebook environment and specified measures; paper includes a later author correction.

stats.population: Consenting U.S. adult Facebook participants with qualifying post-election survey responses
stats.denominator: Study participant sample, not all Facebook users
Exposure to content from sources classified as like-minded relative to the comparison feed
Number of preregistered attitudinal outcomes assessed

title: The Welfare Effects of Social Media
type: Peer-reviewed randomized field experiment; publisher abstract read
findings: Deactivating Facebook for four weeks before the 2018 midterm election reduced factual news knowledge and political polarization, changed time allocation, increased subjective well-being, and reduced subsequent platform use.
limitations: Deactivation removes a broad bundle of social, entertainment, and informational experiences. It does not separately identify the algorithm's political effect. No claim of universal or permanent effects is made in the chapter.

stats.population: Facebook users in the randomized deactivation experiment
stats.denominator: Treatment duration, not a percentage of the electorate

title: Social Media, News Consumption, and Polarization: Evidence from a Field Experiment
type: Peer-reviewed randomized field experiment; publisher abstract read
findings: Random offers of subscriptions to conservative or liberal outlets affected the slant of sites visited. Counter-attitudinal exposure reduced negative attitudes toward the opposing party, while the author found no evidence that outlet leanings changed political opinions. The paper also analyzed the relation between subscriptions and algorithmic delivery.
limitations: The subscription offer and tested outlet choices are specific interventions. Improved attitudes toward an opposing party should not be described as demonstrated changes in policy opinions. Study data-period detail was not extracted from the accessible abstract, so no such date is asserted in the chapter.

title: Bias in Cable News: Persuasion and Polarization
type: Peer-reviewed quasi-experimental and structural-model research; publisher abstract read
findings: The paper exploits cable-channel position as an outside shifter of viewing and estimates a persuasive effect of additional Fox News exposure among affected viewers. A separate model addresses selection, evolving ideology, aggregate influence, and counterfactual slant.
limitations: Channel-placement identification assumptions and the scope of affected viewers matter. Model-based aggregate simulations should not be presented as directly observed national outcomes. The numerical effect is omitted in this chapter to avoid compressing a local estimate into a general claim.

title: Financing dies in darkness? The impact of newspaper closures on public finance
publisher: Journal of Financial Economics 135(2), 445–467; publisher-supplied abstract in RePEc
type: Peer-reviewed quasi-experimental research; original publisher-supplied abstract read in RePEc
findings: The authors report increased municipal borrowing costs after newspaper closures and associate lost monitoring with higher government wages and deficits and more costly financing practices. They argue the identified effect is causal and not explained by underlying economic conditions.
limitations: Publisher page and SSRN blocked browser access; RePEc explicitly identifies publisher-supplied bibliographic content and reproduced the original abstract. Full identification and robustness sections were not inspected. The abstract's 5–11-basis-point and per-issue dollar estimates are deliberately omitted from the chapter because sample-period and financing details were not verified.

title: Press Coverage and Political Accountability
publisher: Journal of Political Economy 118(2), 355–408; accessible NBER Working Paper 13878
type: Original research working-paper abstract with published-version metadata
findings: Uses newspaper-market/congressional-district fit and redistricting variation to study coverage, voter knowledge, representatives' behavior, and policy. Lower coverage is linked to weaker knowledge and differences in congressional activity and federal spending.
limitations: Working-paper abstract and published-version identification were read, not the complete published methods. The chapter describes the causal strategy and its reported results without claiming the design applies to every modern closure or publication.

title: The State of Local News 2026
publisher: Medill Local News Initiative, Northwestern University
type: Original research inventory; executive summary and landscape/methodological discussion read
findings: Reports 238 news-desert counties, over 1,400 additional counties with one remaining local source, and 170 newspapers closed or merged over the preceding year. Discusses startups, philanthropic support, local television newsrooms, and a change incorporating ethnic/foreign-language outlets into their respective categories.
limitations: Counts concern locally based professional sources, not absence of every information source or external broadcast signal. Closures and mergers are combined in the 170 figure. Methodology changed, so simple year-to-year comparisons require attention to classification. Inventory is not itself a causal study of attitudes or governance quality.

stats.population: U.S. counties in Medill's local-news inventory
stats.denominator: Counties without a locally based professional local-news source under the report's definition
Additional counties with only one remaining source; not included among the 238 zero-source counties

stats.population: Newspapers tracked in the local-news inventory
stats.denominator: Count of newspapers closed or merged, not 170 independently verified newsroom closures

title: Trust in Media at New Low of 28% in U.S.
type: Original survey analysis; article and question description read
findings: Reports 28% of U.S. adults expressed a great deal or fair amount of confidence in newspapers, television, and radio to report news fully, accurately, and fairly in its September 2025 survey.
limitations: Measures reported confidence with specific wording, not the measured accuracy of publications. It is a 2025 reading and is labeled as such, not presented as a verified 2026 estimate or as evidence identifying the causes of distrust.

stats.denominator: Respondents expressing a great deal or fair amount of trust/confidence in the specified mass-media reporting question

title: Rescissions Act of 2025, Public Law 119-28, section 2(b)(20)
type: Enacted federal statute; operative provision read
findings: Section 2(b)(20)(A) rescinds amounts made available for CPB for fiscal year 2026 by Public Law 118-47; subparagraph (B) rescinds amounts made available for fiscal year 2027 by Public Law 119-4. The Act was approved July 24, 2025.
limitations: This provision rescinds specified appropriations. It should not be described as prohibiting public-media operations, directly dissolving every local station, or itself proving every subsequent legal winding-up step. No unverified total-dollar figure is asserted.

title: Corporation for Public Broadcasting Board Votes to Dissolve Organization in Act of Responsible Stewardship to Protect the Future of Public Media
publisher: Corporation for Public Broadcasting; original release preserved by Internet Archive
type: Primary institutional announcement; complete release read in a January 5, 2026 archival capture
findings: CPB announced its board had voted to dissolve the corporation following federal defunding. It described an orderly closure, remaining-funds distribution, and archive preservation. The release explicitly distinguishes CPB's ending from continuing local stations, producers, journalists, and educators.
limitations: A board announcement establishes the decision and stated process, not independent proof of when all legal dissolution formalities finished. Statements about motives, political attacks, and institutional benefits are CPB's characterizations and are not adopted as independent causal findings. CPB must be distinguished from NPR, PBS, and local stations.

title: Moody v. NetChoice, LLC, Nos. 22-277 and 22-555
authors: Supreme Court of the United States
publisher: U.S. Supreme Court; opinion reproduced by Cornell Legal Information Institute
type: Primary judicial opinion; syllabus and majority reasoning read
findings: Vacated and remanded the judgments because the lower courts had not properly analyzed the facial First Amendment challenges across the state laws' applications. Explains that selection and curation of third-party speech can constitute protected editorial discretion.
limitations: Not a blanket immunity for all platform functions and not a definitive judgment on every application of the laws. The chapter states the historical 2024 holding and does not claim to establish every later remand development or the current enforceability of every state-law provision.

title: Murthy v. Missouri, No. 23-411
authors: Supreme Court of the United States
publisher: U.S. Supreme Court; opinion reproduced by Cornell Legal Information Institute
type: Primary judicial opinion; syllabus and majority standing analysis read
findings: Held the plaintiffs had not established Article III standing for the prospective injunction sought against government defendants. The majority addressed traceability, likely future injury, and redressability given platforms' independent choices.
limitations: A standing decision, not a general merits holding that all government contacts or pressure are constitutional, or that unlawful coercion never occurs. The chapter does not turn the procedural holding into a conclusion about every alleged instance of moderation pressure.

title: A digital media literacy intervention increases discernment between mainstream and false news in the United States and India
publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
type: Peer-reviewed preregistered survey experiments; original abstract read through Europe PMC
findings: A digital-literacy tips intervention improved discrimination between mainstream and false headlines in a U.S. sample and a highly educated Indian online sample, with different durability and no effect in a largely rural northern Indian sample. Perceived accuracy fell for mainstream headlines as well, but less than for false headlines.
limitations: Headline discernment is not the same as durable civic behavior. Effects differed by population and persistence. The chapter omits percentage improvements to avoid implying identical baselines or universal effects.

title: The effects of Facebook and Instagram on the 2020 election: A deactivation experiment
publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
type: Peer-reviewed randomized deactivation experiments; original abstract read through Europe PMC
findings: Randomized subsets of Facebook and Instagram participants to deactivate for six weeks before the 2020 U.S. election. Effects on issue and affective polarization, perceived election legitimacy, candidate favorability, and turnout were precisely estimated and close to zero. Some other participation and information outcomes changed; the abstract separates secondary analyses and findings not meeting preregistered thresholds.
limitations: Not a test of every historical or long-term platform effect. Volunteer samples, a six-week intervention, and replacement activities limit extrapolation. Findings differ from the 2018-election deactivation study; the chapter does not claim the reasons for that difference are conclusively known.

stats.population: Facebook and Instagram study participants assigned to deactivation
